content_metadata.description: A documentary exploring the influence of astronomers on Pandeism, emphasizing scientific discoveries and theological responses.

qAndA.answer: A rainbow-like spectrum representing the redshift of light from distant galaxies, indicating their movement away from us.
qAndA.question: What visual element is used to represent Edwin Hubble's key discovery about the universe?

qAndA.answer: The Steady State theory, championed by Fred Hoyle.
qAndA.question: Which theory proposed a central point from which new material continuously emerged to fuel the expansion of the universe?

qAndA.answer: Very old quasars and similar ancient, distant structures, not found in the vicinity of younger galaxies.
qAndA.question: What type of astronomical objects provided evidence against the Steady State theory?

qAndA.answer: He recounts an anecdote where a professor's lecture about events shortly after the Big Bang was met with laughter, highlighting the initial skepticism towards these ideas.
qAndA.question: How does Paul Davies describe early reactions to scientific discussions about the Big Bang theory?

qAndA.answer: Pandeism, a view that sees the universe itself as the divine and embraces the scientific understanding of its origins and nature.
qAndA.question: What theological model is presented as aligning with the astronomical discoveries discussed in the video?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Sensure is after Newton, it was astronomers who ensured the upending of Newtonian physics,
when they confirmed Einstein's theory of relativity by observing the predicted gravitational
lensing of light passing distant stars.
It was astronomers who gave us the key to the age of our universe.
Edwin Hubble discovered that ours was not the only galaxy, and by examining the red
shift of other galaxies moving in relation to our own, that the universe was expanding.
It is remarkable in itself that up until 1925, it was not known that a single other galaxy
existed, and after that date, that countless numbers of them did.
Hubble's discovery of universal expansion was disturbing to those who, for both scientific
and theological reasons, believed the universe to have existed forever, in much the same
state.
Astronomer Fred Hoyle was among those who developed the steady state theory, which proposed
that the expansion of our universe was fueled by a constant infusion of new material from
some central point, so that it had always appeared, and would always appear, much as it
does today.
But this theory was disproved with the discovery of very old quasars and similar very old
and very distant structures, not found in the neighborhood of younger galaxies which
are farther along from the point of the initial expansion.
It is somewhat ironic today that the Big Bang proponents were largely religious, championing
the theory in part for its assignment of a point of origin to the universe, which
accorded with creation mythology, while the steady state proponents tended to be atheistic.
Once the Big Bang theory was confirmed, this knowledge, refined over time, allowed
man to at last pinpoint the age of our universe to approximately 13730 million years.
Later astronomers like Carl Saden, Paul Davis and Timothy Ferris would continue to do more
and more, to not only advance our understanding of our universe and the continuum of physics
governing objects within it, but to profoundly affect the validity of theological models as
well, making it impossible to rationally believe in a creator for whom human beings were
at the center of our universe.
I can more remember the professor in my department giving lectures about the early universe, and
talking about how on the basis of this heat radiation it was possible to reconstruct some
of the events that must have occurred only three minutes after the beginning, and everyone
felt about laughing.
They thought this was just a wild speculation.
Nowadays, of course, it's pretty routine to talk not just about the first three minutes,
but even the first three microseconds.
As astronomical discoveries have taken us farther and farther away from our initial
imagined posture in the center of our universe, theological systems have reacted in different
ways.
Some have simply shifted the vanity and self-centeredness, that led us to believe ourselves to be the
center of a perfectly ordered universe away from the astronomical realm, insisting that
even as we are confirmed to occupy an insignificant position in space, we remain the object of
adoration for the creator of that vast space, so richly occupied in places beyond our
very imagination.
Other theological models have strengthened in their grasp of a theology in line with astronomical
reality.
Pandeyism is one such theory, demanding that any theological explanation must accord with
the nature of our observed universe.
And so, the astronomers, in their generations of work advancing our understanding of our
place within our universe, have provided an inspiration to Pandeyism.

youtube_description: This video describes how the astronomers of the Twentieth Century irrevocably disposed humankind of the view of Earth as central to the Universe, eliminating any rational underpinning for theological theories demanding such a central place while providing great inspiration to pandeism.
